overview: Ndé Kónitsąąíí Gokíyaa (Lipan Apache) is an imported atlas label, not a fifteenth-century state, border, or universal self-name. Its only exact feature is a 1492 polygon with 49 positions. It overlaps many labels, so this card treats it as a homeland layer. Evidence distinguishes Southern Athabaskan Ndé people, later Lipan identity, multiple bands, Big Water terminology, and living organizations. A Lipan Apache Women Defense statement translates variant Kónitsąąįį gokíyaa as “Big Water Lipan Country”; TxDOT lists Kónitsąą or Kónitsąą-hii for Lipan Apache people / People of Big Water and separately lists subgroup names. The atlas compound therefore remains ambiguous. Scholarship places Southern Athabaskan ancestors in the Southern Plains archaeological record by 1000 to 1400; Lipan enters writing later. Detailed food, housing, family, healing, diplomacy, and travel evidence is mostly seventeenth century or newer and stays dated below. Eight one-year periods simply divide the atlas interval for evidence review; they are not invented annual events. A 2014 community transcription supplies a small modern language sample, never a 1492 quotation. The exact polygon ends at a software seam. Lipan communities continue.

periods.title: A compound atlas label appears
periods.summary: The exact id is absent in 1400 and appears once in 1492. Its one Polygon carries approximate properties from 1492 to 1500. The file supplies neither a founding event nor evidence that one government, band, population, or exclusive border occupied the whole shape.

periods.title: Overlaps make the boundary nonexclusive
periods.summary: At Austin, Presidio, and El Paso, the target overlaps four other named 1492 features. Six neighboring features share encoded boundary arcs, including two Karankawa features. These measurable intersections make the layer useful for atlas auditing, while ruling out a simple reading as exclusive Lipan political control.

periods.title: Community chronology sets a caution
periods.summary: The Tribe’s retrospective timeline dates Lipan entry into Texas and the development of a Lipan identity to about 1600, then dates two divisions and horse acquisition around 1670. Those community dates cannot be silently replaced with an exact named Lipan polity in this 1494 editorial band.

periods.title: Early comparison is broader Apache evidence
periods.summary: The National Park Service places broadly identified Apache movement into the Texas Panhandle around 1500, then describes Querechos seen in 1541. The page is explicitly about Apaches from 1450 to 1700, so it offers regional comparison without proving that the atlas polygon was Lipan in 1495.

periods.title: Historical names arrive after the interval
periods.summary: Texas Beyond History explains that “Apache” covers several related peoples and discusses Querechos and perhaps Teyas in 1541. It places securely named Lipan in much later documentation. The naming gap prevents converting a broad early account into a precise Lipan observation for 1496.

periods.title: Later descriptions remain later
periods.summary: A UTRGV chapter gathers food, dwelling, clothing, travel, and horse evidence, but its detailed synthesis concerns later Lipan life and relies on historical and ethnographic sources. It helps readers imagine documented practices only when its later date and evidentiary distance from 1497 stay visible.

periods.title: Writing evidence is modern or archival
periods.summary: Robert Soto’s community contribution records modern Lipan lyrics in 2014. The Smithsonian separately catalogs an A. S. Gatschet vocabulary collected at Fort Griffin in 1884. Neither item supplies an alphabetic Lipan sentence authored in 1498, although both document later language work.

periods.title: The software label stops
periods.summary: The compound id disappears in 1500. A different broad Apache layer occupies part of the region then, and a distinct lipan feature appears in 1530. These are changes between atlas source layers, not a dated report of extinction, conquest, migration, or reappearance.

sections.title: Read the map as an overlapping homeland layer

items.text: The only exact feature is one Polygon with one ring, 49 stored positions, and 48 unique vertices. Its decoded bounding box runs roughly from 106.60 degrees west to 96.91 degrees west and 25.16 degrees north to 33.05 degrees north. These are atlas measurements, not Indigenous boundary testimony.

Camp Wood lies inside the target plus Kickapoo, Jumano, and Coahuiltecan layers. Austin lies inside five simultaneous labels; Presidio and El Paso also lie inside five. The overlaps are facts about this map file, not proof that the named peoples shared one government or fixed territorial system.

The exact compound id vanishes in 1500, while a separate lipan id first appears in 1530 with a much smaller shape around central and south Texas. This is a software and source-layer seam. The card does not turn it into a disappearance followed by a return.

A 2009 tribal history page interprets Lipan as “The Light Gray People,” joining łépai, a light gray color, with indeh or ndé, “The People” or “The Tribe.” It is a dated community interpretation. It does not establish the atlas’s full compound phrase as a timeless universal autonym.

The Tribe’s band history describes later divisions, 10 to 14 bands, and rancherías formed from extended families. It lists Kúne tsá as a Big Water band in northern Coahuila. Multiple levels of identity matter: one subgroup name, a homeland phrase, and all Lipan people are not automatically interchangeable.

The tribal timeline places entry into Texas and developing Lipan identity around 1600, a Pecos trade route around 1650, and division plus horse acquisition around 1670. It is community history written long afterward. Its dates challenge, rather than validate, the atlas’s precise 1492 compound label.

The National Park Service’s Alibates page describes broad Apache movement into the Panhandle around 1500. Its 1541 Querechos account belongs to a later encounter and is not labeled Lipan. This regional comparison supports neither an exact 1492 arrival date nor ownership of the atlas polygon.

Texas Beyond History warns that Apache is a generic name for related groups. It discusses Querechos and possibly Teyas encountered in 1541, while placing clearly named Lipan in later records. A reader should keep broad Apache evidence, proposed identifications, and documented Lipan history in separate boxes.

The UTRGV handbook chapter was created with community assistance and compiles later historical and ethnographic descriptions. Its food, clothing, dwelling, and mobility details are useful comparisons, but the chapter does not provide a household diary, census, or excavated Lipan camp securely dated to 1492.

The Smithsonian collection record identifies A. S. Gatschet’s Lipan Apache vocabulary from Fort Griffin, gathered in September and October 1884 across about 46 used pages, including words and some phrases or sentences. It demonstrates later documentation, while supplying no written sample from the atlas interval.

sections.title: Eat, shelter, and travel in dated comparisons

items.text: A tribal history page remembers bison as a primary meat and describes twice-yearly hunts that reunited bands. It also names antelope, deer, rabbits, turkey, quail, and javelina. These are community accounts of Lipan ancestors, recorded in 2009, rather than a dated menu from 1492.

The same community account credits women with gathering and processing cactus fruits, yucca, mescal, tule, palm, mesquite, wild onions, honey, and plums, and with planting corn and squash beside fertile riverbanks. It records remembered work and knowledge without fixing those practices to every fifteenth-century camp.

Leal’s later synthesis describes hide-covered tipis for mobile life and brush or grass wickiups, with a smoke opening at the top. Those dwellings suited movement and available materials. Their documented descriptions postdate the atlas interval, so they illuminate later Lipan practice rather than reconstructing a 1492 house plan.

The UTRGV chapter notes that, before horse adoption, women carried food, shelter materials, and children when communities moved. It also describes clothing differences by age in later evidence. The travel burden is historically meaningful, but the source does not date one particular journey to 1492.

The Tribe’s homeland account dates movement into Texas to the 1600s in search of bison, deer, plants, and riverbank planting places. An NPS site page later connects older routes near San Antonio with Lipan horse expansion. Together they describe later mobility, not ownership of every atlas point.

sections.title: Meet families, bands, and leaders carefully

items.text: The tribal band history defines a ranchería as a group of extended families. A ranchería leader owed allegiance to a band chief, while bands could act together when needed. This retrospective description explains later political scale better than a single-state model and should not be projected unchanged into 1492.

Community history makes major bison hunts social gatherings as well as food work: bands reunited, distant relatives met, and marriages were arranged and celebrated. This warm glimpse of family life comes from a 2009 account of ancestors, not a direct observation made during the atlas years.

Texas Beyond History’s broader Apache synthesis describes close-knit matrilineal extended families, grandparents teaching children, and work shared by age and gender. Because that page combines Apache groups and later records, the pattern is a comparison. It cannot define every Lipan family inside the 1492 polygon.

The Tribe’s biographies are explicitly a non-exhaustive list of later chiefs. They connect leadership with diplomacy, movement, trade, warfare, kinship alliances, and descendants, rather than presenting one permanent throne. Those dated lives show political skill but do not identify a ruler for the fifteenth-century atlas layer.

The story of Kesetta and Jack concerns children captured from a Lipan camp in 1877. The tribal page also disputes uncertain dates, kinship, and leadership claims in later retellings. Its self-correction is a useful lesson: family stories deserve respect, while conflicting details still need labels.

sections.title: Learn across generations and hear modern Lipan

items.text: The Tribe’s current FAQ directs people exploring ancestry toward elders, their stories, family documents, and photographs. It encourages members learning culture and language to speak with elders and attend social events. This is present-day community guidance, not a claim that one unchanged classroom system existed in 1492.

A tribal weapons page says children received arrows with one or two feathers, unlike adult men’s later three-feather arrows. This difference may suggest scaled equipment and learning by doing, but that is an inference. The page does not specify lesson ages, teachers, safety rules, or an exact century for that child practice.

Ashley Leal’s 2024 dissertation treats the Tribe’s powwow as community-based education. Participant observation, informal interviews, and 13 formal interviews identified cultural survival and connectedness, while the event transmitted and transformed knowledge. This is modern Lipan pedagogy and living continuity, not evidence of a 1492 festival.

Modern written sample: “Nii gooyí.” Robert Soto’s May 2014 Lipan Apache musical-lyrics sheet translates it exactly as “There is a good land.” It is a Latin-script community transcription, so transliteration is identical to the written form. The card does not present it as a 1492 quotation.

Mexico’s INALI identifies Ndé miizaa as the Lipan variety within N'dee/N'nee/Ndé and says its alphabet was under review and validation in 2023. It separately describes a community-based language-planning council and interrupted intergenerational transmission. These are current language conditions, not fifteenth-century literacy evidence.

For broad Apache comparison, NPS describes bison providing meat, sinew, bone tools, water containers made from bladder or stomach, dried-dung fuel, and hides for shelter and clothing. The account is anchored to Querechos after 1492 and must not be labeled a complete Lipan toolkit.

The tribal economic history describes later hunters and gatherers who also planted, then traded hides for foods and built intertribal horses-for-guns networks under colonial pressure. By 1800, some bands sold trained horses for cash. Adaptation here means strategic skill, not a simple march from “traditional” to “modern.”

A tribal history of weapons describes later cedar or mulberry bows reinforced with sinew, wooden arrows, buckskin quivers, and a transition from flint to traded metal arrowheads in the early 1700s. It even describes reheating and straightening arrows. None of those dates proves a 1492 assemblage.

At Mission San Lorenzo, archaeology found stone buildings, irrigation ditches, trash middens, thousands of pottery sherds linked to wide trade, and chipped-stone tools. Charred corn and prickly pear also survived. These are remarkable traces of a short colonial mission occupied after 1762, not a precontact Lipan village.

The Tribe’s treaty register lists negotiations with Spain, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the United States, and other nations from 1749 through 1865. The record shows sustained diplomacy under changing colonial regimes. It should be read agreement by agreement, not collapsed into consent to one permanent outside authority.

sections.title: Describe medicine, care, and evidence limits

items.text: Texas Beyond History’s broader and later Apache account says women often served as shamans and describes curing rituals alongside advice and blessings from elders. This is useful comparative evidence, but it neither identifies a Lipan healer in 1492 nor records routine household nursing, pregnancy care, or outcomes.

Morris Opler’s 1938 American Anthropologist article is explicitly about peyote use among Carrizo and Lipan Apache communities. Its 1938 publication places the article centuries after the atlas interval. The title alone does not justify turning a later ceremony into a fifteenth-century prescription or universal practice.

The tribal timeline records smallpox in Lipan camps in 1750 and a devastating epidemic in 1780. Its 1780 entry says Lipan shamans seeking an herbal cure adapted peyote use from Carrizo people. This community chronology links medicine, exchange, and catastrophe, but remains much later than 1492.

A tribal history page says severe smallpox in San Antonio in 1850 drove one ranchería toward Mescalero refuge, while other communities moved to Mexico or hid among Tejano populations. Disease appears here within displacement and family survival, not as an isolated medical episode with reliable case totals.

The Tribe’s current FAQ says it is not federally recognized and therefore lacks much support available to federally acknowledged tribes. It mentions possible health services for some members outside Texas, varying by state. This modern access problem should not be confused with historical healing practice or universal eligibility.

sections.title: Follow water and waste without inventing toilets

items.text: The Alibates NPS page says broadly identified Apache people used dried bison bladders and stomachs as water containers. That ingenious reuse belongs to its later regional comparison. The page does not identify a Lipan household, well, spring, water treatment method, or sanitation rule inside the 1492 shape.

San Lorenzo stood near the Nueces River and a spring, and archaeology records irrigation ditches and trash middens. Water access and discarded material are therefore visible at this later mission. Middens are refuse deposits, not toilets, and Spanish mission infrastructure is not automatically a Lipan sanitation system.

NPS places Mission San Sabá across the river from its presidio and describes green pastures and creeks. A Spanish irrigation canal cut in the 1750s remains visible near the presidio. Those features document a colonial installation; the Lipan visitors refused to settle there, so the canal is not theirs.

The Bustamante treaty records negotiated access to water and pasture, movement, trade, and wild-horse gathering for named Lipan leaders and Mexican officials. It shows that water rights mattered politically in 1822. A treaty entitlement still does not reveal how families carried, stored, shared, or cleaned water.

No reviewed source securely documents a Lipan latrine, toilet location, handwashing rule, menstrual-waste practice, infant-waste routine, or wastewater system for 1492 to 1500. Later mission middens and irrigation cannot fill that gap. The responsible result is a narrow absence statement, not an invented “natural sanitation” story.

sections.title: Face colonial disruption and continued agency

items.text: At San Sabá, NPS says Lipan leaders sought an alliance and protection but thousands gathered for bison hunting and refused to remain at the mission. The mission burned in 1758 during an attack by enemy nations. The episode shows Lipan strategy and choice inside violent colonial and intertribal politics.

The 1822 Bustamante document records peace terms negotiated with named chiefs Cuelgas de Castro and Yolsha Pocarropa. Its articles address movement, exchange, water, pasture, horses, and relations with Comanche people. The treaty is direct documentary evidence of diplomacy, while its promises are not proof of later enforcement.

Texas Historical Commission marker documentation describes the sacred Cementerio del Barrio de los Lipanes at Presidio, links it to a 1790s settlement, records 45 identified graves, and notes descendants on both sides of the border. The cemetery material anchors family continuity without turning every burial into an identified biography.

The Tribe’s reservation-era account traces small groups toward Mescalero, Oklahoma, and Mexico while others remained hidden in Texas and blended into Tejano communities. Spanish surnames and movement complicated official visibility. Dispersal under coercion changed where records found people; it did not make Lipan families disappear.

The Tribe’s treaty page begins with an August 1749 agreement with Spain and follows negotiations through Mexico, Texas, the United States, and an 1865 intertribal compact. Reading the sequence reveals repeated political action under pressure. It also prevents one document from being mistaken for permanent surrender or recognition.

sections.title: Meet living communities without merging organizations

items.text: Texas Senate Concurrent Resolution 61 recognizes the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas and describes government, community service, military service, and contributions. It is a 2019 state action, not federal acknowledgement and not evidence for a 1492 border. The modern organization should remain distinct from other Lipan groups.

The National Park Service land and water acknowledgement names Lipan Apache among non-federally recognized San Antonio groups with enduring ties to mission places. It also distinguishes federally recognized associated nations and other descendant communities. The page supports living connection while warning readers not to merge different peoples or legal statuses.

The Tribe distinguishes its government from nonprofit instrumentalities serving cultural, educational, health, land, language, cemetery, and public-learning purposes. That organizational detail makes continuity concrete. A cultural card can acknowledge present institutions without pretending every nonprofit, band, association, and tribal government is the same legal body.

The current FAQ bases enrollment on descent, directs families toward elders and records, encourages members to learn through elders and social events, and says spoken-language restoration is underway. These are modern community practices. They should not be rewritten as unchanged fifteenth-century citizenship rules or a completed language revival.

The Lipan Apache Tribe Cemetery Association describes preserving the Presidio cemetery, transfers, and repatriation work. Care for ancestors and burial places is active community labor, not merely an archaeological afterword. The association is one institution within a wider Lipan world and should not stand in for every descendant organization.

ending.text: The exact compound layer ends at 1500 because the atlas changes source layers, not because a historical source reports the Lipan people’s defeat or disappearance. In 1500, broader Apache and other regional labels replace the target. By 1530, the atlas draws a distinct lipan feature with a different footprint. Neither seam is a trustworthy migration date. The Tribe’s community history instead follows later Lipan bands through colonial warfare, epidemics, food shortages, cross-border movement, coercion, and survival. It describes people who went to New Mexico and Oklahoma, many who remained free, and families who survived in enclave communities such as San Antonio’s Indian Town. It remembers Little Breech Cloth and Tall Grass Band communities, elders telling children never to forget they were Lipan Apache, and current tribal members as one united Indigenous community. This is one present organization’s account, not a claim that every Lipan descendant or organization is legally identical. The maps cannot decide those relationships. The atlas polygon was never a surveyed national border, and its eight-year lifespan cannot measure a people’s lifetime. The evidence supports living continuity through disruption, with the software endpoint kept separate from human history.
